name: Peer-to-Peer Networks
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: No One in Charge: How Peer-to-Peer Networks Distribute Control
lesson.summary: Contrasts peer-to-peer networks with the client-server model, showing how removing a central server improves resilience but shifts the burden of verifying trust and reaching agreement onto the peers themselves.
lesson.body:
Peer-to-peer, or P2P, networks take a different approach from the client-server model covered in the last chapter. Instead of dividing participants into clients that request and servers that respond, a peer-to-peer network treats every participating computer, or peer, as roughly equal: each one can both request information from other peers and supply information to them. There is no single server that all requests must pass through, and no single operator whose servers, if shut down, would take the whole network down with them.

File-sharing networks popularized the model publicly in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Rather than downloading a file from one company's central server, as in the client-server model, a peer-to-peer file-sharing system like BitTorrent lets a user download small pieces of a file simultaneously from many other peers who already have those pieces, while also uploading pieces to others who need them. Because the file exists as copies scattered across many independent peers rather than one server, the network keeps working even as individual peers join, leave, or go offline, and there is no single company whose decision to shut down its servers ends access for everyone.

This distributed structure changes where trust has to live. In a client-server system, users trust one identifiable, accountable operator. In a peer-to-peer system, there is no equivalent central party to hold accountable, which removes a single point of failure but also removes a single point of responsibility. Peers connecting to strangers' machines have to contend with the digital trust problem in its rawest form: how do you know the peer sending you data is sending what it claims, has not tampered with it, or is not simply absent when you need it? Peer-to-peer systems generally answer this with technical measures, such as checking data against a known cryptographic fingerprint after downloading, rather than by trusting the sender's word.

Coordination is also harder without a central authority. A server can simply decide the current, authoritative state of things, such as your bank balance, because it is the sole keeper of the record. A peer-to-peer network, with many independent copies and no single authoritative keeper, has to find some other way for peers to agree on shared facts, especially when different peers might have received conflicting or outdated information. This coordination problem, reaching agreement across many independent, mutually distrustful participants without a central referee, turns out to be one of the hardest problems in distributed computing, and it is the exact problem that blockchain systems, covered in later chapters, were designed to address for the specific case of tracking who owns what.

For now, the key takeaway is structural: client-server and peer-to-peer are two different answers to the same underlying question, who is trusted to keep the authoritative record, and each answer carries real tradeoffs in convenience, accountability, and resilience rather than one simply being better than the other.
